meta.title: Minimal SIP client: what RFC 3261 subset is sufficient to register and hold a call with a real PBX?
meta.question: What subset of RFC 3261 is necessary and sufficient for a from-scratch SIP client to register, establish, and tear down a two-way RTP call against a mainstream PBX?

pitch.one_line_answer: A from-scratch SIP client needs only 90 of RFC 3261's 540 normative must-statements (16.7%) to register, call, hold, resume and hang up against a real PBX — and resumes a held call's media where the reference stack's own API cannot (E-007, E-008).
pitch.elevator: SIP (RFC 3261) is a 300-page protocol, and a production stack carries all of it: forking, presence, encryption, timers, retransmissions, S/MIME. This repository asks how much of that is actually load-bearing for one ordinary job — a client that registers with a PBX, makes a two-way audio call, puts it on hold, brings it back, and hangs up. We built that client from zero, with no SIP library, and then enumerated, statement by statement, which of the protocol's normative requirements the scenarios actually force. The answer: 90 of 540, or 16.7% (E-007). The reference stack, PJSIP 2.17, completes the same suite — and its own high-level API cannot restart a held call's media without a sound device, while the 1,100-line client here can (E-008).

hypotheses.statement: Under the scenario suite (register, two-way RTP call, hold/resume, teardown against a pinned Asterisk version), a from-scratch SIP client requires fewer than half of RFC 3261's normative MUST requirements to complete the same suite that PJSIP 2.17 completes in full, at the cost of not supporting SIP features outside the suite (forking, presence, subscription).

headline.text: 16.7% — the fraction of RFC 3261's normative must-statements (90 of 540) a client needs to complete the whole scenario suite, 33 points under the 50% falsifier line (E-007).
102/102 — RTP packets exchanged after a held call resumes, where the reference stack's own API returns no media stream at all in the same headless environment (E-008).
32 s — exactly how long the client takes to notice a PBX killed mid-call: media stops, the hangup times out at the protocol's own 64×T1 bound, and the client exits cleanly (E-006).

integrations.note: RFC 3261 over UDP 5060 plus RTP (PCMU) — protocol and contract named (D-001, README public interface, matrix) and exercised end-to-end against the real pinned PBX (E-004): register, call, hold/resume, teardown. Error semantics defined and unit-tested (timeouts 64xT1 -> 408, Timer E retransmission, CSeq idempotency, 401 digest retry on REGISTER and INVITE — E-003). Lifecycle handled in code (connect via probe+register, dialog manage via re-INVITE, terminate via BYE + Close, resource release on stream/conn close) and exercised in the suite. Blocked from IRL 6: single codec, single concurrent call — end-to-end flow under realistic volumes and edge encodings is unexercised, and there is no fault injection against the real PBX (unit-tier faults run against the fake UAS only).

The host seam: the compiled client runs inside the golang:1.22-alpine container and the suite exits with the client's exit code (compose --exit-code-from client, propagated by run-suite.sh). Contract documented (README Try it, Makefile suite target); error semantics defined (exit 0 = suite passed, non-zero otherwise). Blocked from IRL 5: the container's shutdown path (SIGTERM handling, drain of an in-flight call before exit) is untested — compose stops the container after the suite finishes, so graceful termination at the host seam is not proven.

journey.title: What the protocol actually demands
journey.summary: A full survey of RFC 3261 found 590 normative must-occurrences across every section — and a suspicion that almost none of them are needed for an ordinary call. The falsification line was fixed in advance: if completing the suite forces a majority of them, the claim is wrong.

journey.title: A working call against a real PBX
journey.summary: The first client registered, called, held, resumed and tore down against a real Asterisk container — media flowed both ways (152/152). That proved the scenario suite was completable, not that the subset was small.

journey.title: A client worth auditing
journey.summary: The client was rebuilt as a small, auditable component with the wire trace recorded on every message — and the trace became the instrument: each behaviour carries the RFC section that forces it, so the subset is enumerable rather than asserted.

journey.title: Counting what the suite forces
journey.summary: The enumeration came in at 90 of 540 statements (16.7%), with two stricter counting rules also far under the line. The 590-occurrence text never needed to be reached — the claim held under the rule that should have caught inflation.

journey.title: The incumbent, run head to head
journey.summary: PJSIP 2.17 built from source, same suite, same PBX, five runs each — and one genuine finding: its high-level API cannot restart a held call's media headless. The client here can, and the limitation is reported rather than tuned away.

dead_ends.title: The INVITE that forgot its body
dead_ends.text: The first client sent its INVITE with Content-Length: 0 — no SDP at all. The call "succeeded" and no media ever flowed. Only the integration suite against the real PBX caught it; the regression test that guards it now is part of the suite (E-004).

dead_ends.title: The re-INVITE that collided with itself
dead_ends.text: A hold re-INVITE reused the CSeq of the initial INVITE after the digest retry — the PBX answered 491 Request Pending. The dialog CSeq has to be the one actually used on the wire, not the one the code intended. A property test now pins the invariant.

dead_ends.title: The baseline that could not come back from hold
dead_ends.text: Getting PJSIP 2.17's Python API to restart a held call's media headless ate the longest debug stretch of the comparison: its unhold offers a port-0 loopback (488), media re-initialisation crashes, and a manual offer leaves the stream inactive. The endpoint is a documented limitation (E-008), not a fix — and the client here does the step the incumbent cannot.

lessons: A protocol standard is not a load-bearing surface: most of RFC 3261's normative requirements exist for deployments this scenario cannot touch — proxies, forking, encryption, presence, S/MIME.

Deciding the falsifier before measuring is what keeps the result honest: at 16.7%, the temptation is to loosen the counting; the pre-registered 50% line is why nobody can accuse the number of being tuned.

Running the incumbent under the same conditions is a measurement instrument of its own: it surfaced a real pjsua2 limitation (no headless media restart) that no amount of code reading would have found.
Record the wire, not the intention: the message trace turned a pass/fail suite into an audit trail, and that trail is the paper backing every number in this repository.

limitations.baseline_wins: For breadth, the incumbent wins outright: PJSIP ships forking, presence, TCP/TLS, every codec and two decades of field hardening. A general-purpose communications product should use PJSIP; the only claim here is about the size of the load-bearing subset (E-008).
limitations.untested: Interop is proven against exactly one PBX (a pinned Asterisk 20); media is one client against Asterisk's Echo() with no second real endpoint; only UDP and PCMU are implemented, so a PBX that demands TLS or another codec will not complete the suite (R-001, R-002, R-004).
limitations.next_level: The next readiness level needs a production-like environment: a second real endpoint, a load generator, sustained multi-call traffic, and monitoring. Nothing in this suite provides those yet.
limitations.structural: The client is a measurement instrument first. An engineer solving the call problem with PJSIP loses nothing by using SIP — the point of this repository is the 16.7% and the matrix behind it, not the client.

audience.who_is_this_for: Engineers who want to know which parts of a 300-page protocol are actually load-bearing for an ordinary client scenario — and anyone building a minimal SIP endpoint (embedded, scenario-based, or educational) who wants the auditable statement-by-statement list.
audience.not_for: Not a library for a general-purpose product: no forking, no TLS, one codec, one proven PBX. And not a tutorial — it is a measurement with a working example attached.
